strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical analysis extending infinite-width and infinite-depth parameterisation theory (µP/mean-field, developed originally for BP) to predictive coding networks, proving that the same set of stable and feature-learning parameterisations applies to both algorithms (Theorems 1 and 2). This is a nontrivial, technically careful generalization that goes beyond prior work (e.g., Ishikawa et al. 2024, which only showed existence of such a parameterisation, not necessity/uniqueness).

The theoretical results are accompanied by a convergence result (Corollaries 3.2 and 4.2) showing PC gradients converge to BP gradients when width >> depth, giving a precise, falsifiable, and intuitive characterization of when/why PC approximates BP for linear networks.

Strong empirical validation across a wide range of settings: linear MLPs/ResNets, nonlinear MLPs (Tanh, ReLU), CNNs on ImageNet, and transformers on Tiny Shakespeare, with consistent support for the theoretical predictions, including under different optimizers (SGD, Adam) and losses (MSE, cross-entropy). The appendix is unusually thorough with detailed derivations and many supplementary figures/ablations.

Clear articulation of practical implications: identifies that widely-used PC parameterisations (relying on SP) are provably unstable at large width/depth, offers a principled alternative, and connects results to plausible neuroscience relevance (brain being wide relative to depth) and potential hardware-based inference speedups.

Honest, detailed discussion of limitations (linear theory, PC inference cost, biologically implausible attention, lack of training-to-convergence experiments) rather than glossing over weaknesses, which increases the credibility of the contribution.
weaknesses: The core theoretical results (Theorems 1-2, Corollaries 3.2-4.2) are restricted to linear networks with exactly equilibrated activities; while nonlinear experiments are supportive, there is no theoretical bridge (e.g., via DMFT) to nonlinear networks, so the generality of the 'PC = BP under width>>depth' claim for practical models rests entirely on empirical demonstration rather than proof.

All experiments are trained for very few steps (100 steps per the appendix), explicitly acknowledged as a limitation; this leaves open whether the observed alignment persists with longer training, at convergence, or translates into actual competitive task performance (accuracy, perplexity) versus BP-trained models.

The practical takeaway is somewhat double-edged: the paper shows that scaling PC requires width >> depth, which is precisely the regime where PC becomes computationally most expensive relative to BP (inference cost scaling with width) and where the unique advantages of PC (e.g., fast saddle-to-saddle dynamics) disappear (Takeaway 2), raising questions about the practical value/motivation of pursuing this direction further, an issue that is honestly discussed but somewhat undercuts the significance of the contribution.

Some experimental design choices are questionable for generalizability, e.g. the transformer experiments explicitly remove layer normalization because it breaks convergence to BP, and the attention mechanism used is noted to be biologically non-local -- weakening the paper's claims about biological plausibility of the overall approach and about scalability to real, practical transformer architectures.

The paper's central 'negative' framing (PC-under-stable-parameterisation strictly converges to BP) means the work does not identify a case where PC offers a genuine computational or statistical advantage over BP in the stable/scalable regime; the interesting result identified elsewhere (fast saddle-to-saddle dynamics) is shown to be unstable under scaling, somewhat limiting the positive contribution to a proof that a known biologically-plausible algorithm can reduce to a known algorithm under specific conditions.

strengths: The theoretical derivation is careful and detailed (full proofs in the appendix spanning width and depth scalings), extending the µP/mean-field tensor-programs-style analysis to predictive coding networks in a rigorous way.

The paper clearly identifies the exact set of width- and depth-stable, feature-learning parameterisations for linear PCNs and shows it coincides with the BP set (Theorems 1-2), which is a non-trivial generalization of prior partial results by Ishikawa et al. (2024) and Innocenti et al. (2025).

The empirical validation is broad, spanning linear MLPs/ResNets, nonlinear MLPs/ResNets, CNNs on ImageNet, and transformers on Tiny Shakespeare, lending some credibility to the claim that the linear theory extends qualitatively to practical nonlinear architectures.

The writing is generally clear, the desiderata-based framework is well organized, and the paper is transparent about several of its own limitations (linear theory, PC inference cost, lack of training-to-convergence results).
weaknesses: The core theoretical results are restricted to linear networks with exactly equilibrated activities; the extension to nonlinear architectures (CNNs, transformers) relies entirely on heuristic parameterisation choices and cosine-similarity diagnostics rather than any formal guarantee, so the central claims about 'hard constraints' on scalable PC parameterisations are not actually established for the architectures practitioners care about.

The paper's main positive finding is essentially that, under the derived parameterisation, PC collapses onto BP when width greatly exceeds depth — i.e., PC offers no computational or statistical advantage over BP in the regime where it is theoretically tractable. Combined with Takeaway 2 (the one previously-known PC-specific benefit, fast saddle-to-saddle dynamics, is shown to be unstable at scale), the paper's net contribution reads as largely negative/confirmatory rather than opening a genuinely new capability for PC.

Experiments are run for only 100 training steps (acknowledged in §6.3), with no demonstration that PC can be trained to convergence and match BP performance on a non-trivial task; this leaves the core motivating promise of the paper (that biologically-plausible local learning can match BP in practice) empirically unsupported.

The transformer experiments required removing layer normalisation to observe convergence to BP, which is a significant deviation from standard architectures and undermines confidence that the theory/parameterisation transfers to modern practical transformer stacks.

The inference cost of PC — the main practical bottleneck preventing any real benefit from the parallelizable weight updates — is not addressed at all in this paper; up to 100k inference steps were needed for convergence in some experiments, which makes the claimed implication ('BP can be effectively implemented with only local updates... sped up by a factor of L') largely aspirational rather than demonstrated.

No hyperparameter-transfer experiments are performed despite this being a central practical payoff of µP-style parameterisations for BP and a claimed future benefit for PC; the paper only predicts transfer would hold without testing it.

Some claims (e.g., the brain analogy, PC as a plausible model of cortical computation given these results) are speculative and not tightly connected to the technical content, which is purely about artificial network training dynamics under idealized gradient flow/GD.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical extension of the infinite width/depth parameterisation framework (µP/mean-field) from BP to predictive coding networks, proving that the set of width- and depth-stable feature-learning parameterisations coincides exactly for PC and BP (Theorems 1 and 2). This is a nontrivial generalization that goes beyond prior existence results (e.g., Ishikawa et al. 2024) to a necessity/uniqueness claim.

The theoretical results are clearly connected to practical prior work (e.g., µPC of Innocenti et al. 2025), providing a more principled justification for empirically successful heuristic reparameterisations used to scale PC to 100+ layer networks.

The paper supports its linear theory with a reasonably broad set of empirical validations across architectures (MLPs, CNNs, transformers), datasets (CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST, ImageNet, Tiny Shakespeare), and optimisers (GD, Adam), showing that the theoretical predictions approximately hold even for nonlinear models in practice.

The derivations are detailed and appear mathematically careful, with extensive appendices deriving scaling exponents for each desideratum, and useful asymptotic lemmas (e.g., feature/gradient kernel concentration, equilibrated energy rescaling behavior) that could be reused in follow-up work.

The discussion section is unusually candid about limitations (linearity, inference cost, biologically implausible attention, partial training to convergence) and ethically appropriate, framing the contribution honestly as both a constraint (negative result bounding useful parameterisations) and a positive result (a path for local algorithms to implement BP in wide-shallow networks, relevant to neuroscience and efficient hardware).
The connection to brain architecture (wide, shallow) and modern LLMs (also wide relative to depth) adds a compelling significance/motivation angle beyond pure theory.
weaknesses: The central theoretical results (Theorems 1 and 2, Corollaries 3.2 and 4.2) are restricted to linear networks with exactly equilibrated activities, which is a strong assumption; the extension to nonlinear networks is only empirically supported, not theoretically justified via e.g. DMFT, which the authors acknowledge but leave as future work.

The practical implication of the convergence result is somewhat deflationary: PC essentially reduces to BP under the derived parameterisations and in the N≫L regime, meaning the paper does not demonstrate a new computational advantage of PC, and in fact previously identified PC benefits (fast saddle-to-saddle dynamics) are shown to be unstable under scaling.

Experiments are run for very few training steps (100 steps, as explicitly noted in the limitations), which leaves open how well the convergence/alignment result and the practical utility of these parameterisations hold with longer training or at convergence, especially for tasks like ImageNet or language modeling where only early-training cosine similarities are reported rather than final performance comparisons.

The CNN and transformer parameterisation extensions are explicitly described as heuristic rather than derived from the same rigorous analysis as the MLP/ResNet case, somewhat weakening the generality claims for architectures most relevant to current large-scale deep learning.

The required large number of PC inference steps for convergence (up to 100k for deep models, per appendix) underscores that the computational practicality of this approach remains an open and potentially serious bottleneck, which is acknowledged but not resolved.

While the authors argue the result constrains the scalable parameterisation space to be identical to µP, the paper's discussion itself concedes that other, differently-constrained notions of stability (e.g., inference landscape conditioning) might not converge to BP, so the strength of the 'necessarily' claim in the discussion could be viewed as somewhat overstated relative to the acknowledged caveat.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of infinite width and depth limits for predictive coding networks (PCNs), extending the well-established BP-parameterisation theory (µP/mean-field) to PC for the first time in a comprehensive way. Theorems 1 and 2 are proved with careful derivations covering all three stability/feature-learning desiderata for width and two for depth, going beyond prior work (Ishikawa et al. 2024) which only showed existence of such a parameterisation rather than uniqueness.

The central result that PC and BP share exactly the same class of stable, feature-learning parameterisations is surprising and practically important: it implies that PCNs trained with standard (PyTorch-style) initialisation are provably unstable at large width/depth, which has direct implications for the growing literature on scaling PCNs (µPC, ePC, etc.).

The convergence results (Corollaries 3.2 and 4.2) are non-trivial generalisations of prior partial results (e.g., Innocenti et al. 2025 only showed convergence at initialization), and are given with explicit rates (O(1/N) and O(L/N)) derived from careful asymptotic analysis of the equilibrated energy rescaling term.

Empirical validation is broad and goes beyond the linear theory: experiments span linear and nonlinear MLPs, residual networks, CNNs (ImageNet-1k) and transformers (Tiny Shakespeare), with consistent high gradient alignment between PC and BP for wide/shallow architectures, lending credibility to the claim that the theoretical results are practically relevant beyond the idealized linear setting.

The paper is transparent about limitations (linear theory, PC inference cost, short training runs, non-local attention) and offers a clear discussion of implications for both scalable ML systems and biological plausibility (brain being wide relative to depth), which strengthens the significance and honesty of the contribution.
Code availability is mentioned for reproducibility, and the appendix provides extensive derivations and additional experiments supporting the main claims.
weaknesses: The core theoretical machinery relies entirely on linear networks with exact activity equilibrium, which is a substantial idealization; the nonlinear experiments, while supportive, are heuristic extensions (§A.7) without formal guarantees, and the training runs are very short (100 steps), leaving open whether the theory's predictions (including hyperparameter transfer, a major practical benefit of µP) actually hold at scale or over longer training horizons for nonlinear PCNs.

The paper's main finding is in some sense a negative result for PC's distinctiveness: under the derived stable/rich parameterisations, PC essentially collapses to BP as width grows, and the one regime where PC was shown to provide genuine benefit over BP (fast saddle-to-saddle dynamics, Takeaway 2) is explicitly shown to be unstable under the very scalable parameterisations being proposed. This tempers the practical value of the contribution for using PC as an alternative to BP with genuine benefits.

PC's fundamental limitation—the cost of running inference to convergence—is not resolved or substantially mitigated by this work; the paper's own experiments needed up to 100k inference steps for the deepest models (§A.9), and the manuscript acknowledges this remains an open and possibly more important bottleneck than the parameterisation question addressed here.

The claim that 'necessarily µP is the only scalable parameterisation for PC' is explicitly caveated as being relative to the specific abcd-parameterisation family considered (§2.2) and the specific desiderata employed; the possibility of other stable/rich parameterisations under different constraints is left open (Figure A.5), which somewhat weakens the strength of the 'necessarily' framing in the main text.

The hyperparameter-transfer property—arguably the most practically valuable consequence of µP-style parameterisations for BP—is explicitly not validated in this paper (mentioned as future work), so the practical payoff of the theoretical results for actually scaling PC training in practice remains unconfirmed.

The removal of layer normalization for the transformer experiments (noted to break PC-BP convergence) suggests the correspondence may be fragile to common architectural components, raising questions about the generality of the gradient-alignment findings to standard modern architectures used in practice.

strengths: The theoretical core (Theorems 1-2) is derived with careful, exhaustive rigor for linear MLPs and residual networks, extending the established μP/mean-field machinery (Yang & Hu; Bordelon & Pehlevan) to the PC setting in a technically sound way, with full derivations in the appendix.

The paper clearly identifies and fills a genuine gap: prior PC scaling work (e.g. μPC) was heuristic, and this paper supplies the first principled characterization of which parameterizations are simultaneously stable and feature-learning for PC.

The convergence results (Corollaries 3.2 and 4.2) are non-trivial generalizations of prior partial results (e.g. Innocenti et al. 2025 only showed convergence at initialization; this paper shows it throughout training with explicit rate bounds).

Empirical validation spans a reasonable range of settings for a theory paper: linear networks, nonlinear MLPs/ResNets, CNNs on ImageNet, and transformers on Tiny Shakespeare, with consistent qualitative agreement with the theory.

The limitations section is unusually thorough and honest, explicitly flagging the linear-only theory, inference cost, lack of training-to-convergence experiments, and non-local attention as open issues.
weaknesses: The rigorous theory is confined entirely to linear networks; the extension to nonlinear CNNs/transformers is admitted to be 'heuristic' (§A.7) with no formal guarantees, so the paper's title/framing promising general PCN scaling laws overstates what is actually proven.

The central finding is essentially deflationary: under any parameterization satisfying the stability/feature-learning desiderata, PC provably collapses to BP in the relevant wide limit, and the one regime where PC was previously shown to outperform BP (fast saddle-to-saddle dynamics) is shown to be unstable with both width and depth (Takeaway 2). This leaves limited positive, actionable guidance for practitioners wanting to exploit PC's purported advantages.

All experiments (including the 'large-scale' ImageNet CNN) are run for only 100 training steps with tiny channel counts (Cout up to 32), so no evidence is given that PC trained under these parameterizations actually reaches competitive task performance, only that gradients are cosine-aligned with BP early in training.

The paper does not address the well-known PC inference-cost bottleneck in its own experiments (inference required up to 100k steps for deep models per §A.9), undermining the claimed practical relevance ('O(1) rather than O(L) weight-update cost') since this benefit is never empirically realized.

Gradient cosine similarity is the only metric used to support convergence claims on nonlinear architectures; no loss/accuracy comparisons between PC and BP trained models are reported, which would be a more decisive test of practical equivalence.

Presentation is extremely dense, with the main text relying heavily on a 25-page appendix for essentially all derivations and most supporting figures, making the core contribution hard to assess without extensive cross-referencing.

The claim that 'the brain is much wider than deep' is used to motivate biological relevance, but the paper's own theory only applies to a narrow, specific family of 'abcd' parameterizations and linear dynamics, so the leap to biological plausibility claims is speculative and under-supported.

strengths: Rigorous and carefully derived theoretical extension of the width/depth infinite-limit parameterization framework (μP/mean-field, as developed for BP by Yang & Hu and Bordelon & Pehlevan) to predictive coding networks, yielding clean theorems (Thm 1, 2) that the stable and feature-learning parameterization set for PC coincides exactly with that for BP.

Non-trivial convergence results with explicit rates (O(1/N) for MLPs, O(L/N) for residual nets) that generalize and strengthen prior partial results (e.g., Ishikawa et al. 2024 only showed existence of a parameterization; Innocenti et al. 2025 only showed initialization-time convergence).

Thorough empirical validation across a wide range of settings: linear and nonlinear MLPs/ResNets/CNNs/transformers, multiple datasets (toy, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet, Tiny Shakespeare), multiple optimizers and nonlinearities, with results broadly consistent with the theory (Figures 1-4 and extensive appendix figures).
Practically important and actionable conclusion: standard (PyTorch-style) PC parameterizations are unstable with width/depth, which has direct implications for how PC should be scaled in practice.
Good situating of the work relative to closely related prior papers (Ishikawa et al. 2024, Innocenti et al. 2025, Goemaere et al. 2025), with explicit, well-argued statements of what is new.

Honest and detailed limitations/future-work section (linear theory restriction, PC inference cost, lack of training-to-convergence experiments, non-local attention) that does not overstate the contribution.

Interesting conceptual link to biological plausibility (brains are wider than deep), providing a motivating narrative for why the wide/shallow convergence result could be relevant beyond pure ML scaling.
weaknesses: The core theoretical results are restricted to linear networks; the extension to nonlinear architectures (CNNs, transformers) is only heuristic/empirical, with no analytical guarantees, and the authors acknowledge a DMFT-based generalization is left to future work.

Practical demonstration is limited to very short training runs (100 steps), so the paper does not show PC trained to convergence can match BP performance at scale, limiting the strength of the 'scalability' claims made in the abstract/intro.

The main previously-claimed advantage of PC over BP (fast saddle-to-saddle dynamics) is shown to be unstable under scalable parameterizations, somewhat undercutting the broader motivation for using PC over BP, though this is presented honestly.

PC inference remains computationally expensive (up to 100k steps needed for the deepest models to converge in experiments), and the paper does not resolve or substantially mitigate this bottleneck, which is arguably the central practical obstacle to applying the theory.

Some gap between the theoretically justified exponents and the heuristic per-architecture extensions (CNNs, transformers, Adam) used in experiments, which are not derived with the same rigor as the MLP/ResNet case, slightly weakening the tightness of theory-experiment correspondence.

Reproducibility is not fully verifiable from the text alone (the code repository link appears truncated/missing in the provided document), though the appendix experimental details are otherwise fairly thorough.

Dense, notation-heavy presentation (appropriate for a theory paper) may limit accessibility to readers less familiar with tensor-programs/DMFT style analyses, though this is a minor concern relative to the paper's main audience.
